q: A small app has 2 servers, a database, a load balancer and a NAT gateway. In the lesson's example bill (AWS prices read on 2026-11-19), which line is the biggest?
options: The NAT gateway, because it costs hours and every GB through it
The 2 servers
The database
The load balancer
why: The gateway costs $0.045 an hour (about $32.85 a month) just for being there, plus $0.045 for every GB. In the example it is $41.85, more than the two servers ($30.37). The prices are examples and change.

q: Which of these cost money even when nobody uses the app?
options: A load balancer that gets no requests
A NAT gateway with no traffic
A disk that is not attached to any server
A server that was stopped and deleted, with nothing left behind
why: Hours-based and stored things keep billing: the load balancer and the NAT gateway bill every hour they exist, and a disk bills for its GB attached or not. A deleted server with nothing left behind bills nothing.

q: A NAT gateway is billed only for the GB that go through it. With no traffic it is free.
why: It has two meters: an hourly charge for being there, and a charge for each GB processed. With zero traffic you still pay the hours.

q: A server costs $0.0208 an hour on demand. A month has 730 hours. Type the monthly cost with a dollar sign, rounded to cents.
why: 0.0208 x 730 = 15.184, which is $15.18. Two of these servers are $30.37 in the lesson's bill.

q: Data coming in to AWS from the internet and data going out to the internet are charged the same way.
why: The charge is for data going out (egress). In the lesson's example the first 100 GB a month are free and the rest cost $0.09 a GB. Check the current price page for details.

q: A one year plan costs 62.5 percent of the on demand price per hour, and bills every hour. A server runs half of the month. Which is cheaper?
options: On demand, because the plan bills the hours the server is off
The plan, because the price per hour is lower
They cost the same
It depends on the region only
why: On demand costs 0.5 x 100 percent = 50 percent of a full month. The plan costs 62.5 percent. The plan wins only above the break-even share, which here is 62.5 percent of the hours.

q: A plan costs $0.013 an hour. On demand costs $0.0208 an hour. Type the break-even share (the share of hours the server must run for the plan to win) as a decimal.
why: The break-even share is plan price divided by on demand price: 0.013 / 0.0208 = 0.625. Above 62.5 percent use, the plan is cheaper.

q: Put the ways to cut a bill in the order the lesson recommends.
items: Buy a one year plan for the steady rest
why: Delete the waste first, then use less, then pay a lower price per hour. The plan comes last, so you do not promise a year of waste.

q: A team buys a 3 year plan for 4 big servers. Two months later they find the servers are mostly empty and shrink them to 2 small ones. What happens to the plan?
options: They still pay the promise, so some of it buys nothing
AWS cancels the plan and refunds the rest
The price per hour drops to match the new servers
The plan moves to another account for free
why: A plan is a promise to pay for a set amount of compute every hour for the whole term. The AWS docs say the terms cannot be changed after purchase. Right size first, then commit.

q: Which jobs fit Spot instances (spare servers at a discount, taken back with a two minute warning)?
options: A batch job that can start again from a saved step
A video converter that processes a queue of small tasks
The only copy of your production database
The only server that answers your customers
why: Spot can be interrupted, so use it for work that can stop and restart. Never use it for the only copy of something that must stay up.

q: In the lesson's bill, 120 of the 200 GB through the NAT gateway are uploads to S3. What is the cheapest fix that keeps the app working?
options: Add an S3 gateway endpoint, which has no extra charge, so those GB skip the NAT gateway
Buy a bigger NAT gateway
Turn off logging
Move the servers to another region
why: A gateway endpoint for S3 is a private route with no additional charge (AWS docs). The traffic no longer passes the NAT gateway, so the per GB charge for it goes away. The hourly charge stays.

q: If you tag all your resources with app=shop today, you can group the bill by that tag in the next hour.
why: You must activate the tag as a cost allocation tag in the billing console, and the AWS docs say tags can take up to 24 hours to appear.

q: A budget alert at 80 percent of actual spend fires on day 17 of the month. What is the best extra alert to add so you hear about a jump sooner?
options: An alert on the forecasted spend
An alert at 200 percent of the budget
No alert, check the bill at month end
An alert on the number of servers only
why: AWS Budgets can alert on forecasted spend as well as actual spend. A forecast alert can come days before the actual total reaches the line. Alerts still tell you only. Someone must fix the cause.
